(CNN) -- The space shuttle Atlantis crew completed its first spacewalk to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope, a daylong act of grueling labor that featured the replacement and installation of key instruments. Spacewalkers remove a camera from the Hubble on Thursday. Astronauts John Grunsfeld and Drew Feustel removed the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and swapped it out with an updated model, a device that "will allow the telescope to take large-scale, clear and detailed photos over a wide range of colors," NASA said. But they had a tough time removing a bolt in that task, an issue that caused some concern for colleagues on the ground. They eventually released it. "OK, here we go. I think I got it. It turned. It turned. And it's turning easily now," Feustel said. "Very nice." In all, the repair mission took seven hours and 20 minutes, a hard day's work that ended at 4:12 p.m. EDT. "It turned out very well," lead flight director Tony Ceccacci said during a NASA briefing. The team also replaced a Science Instrument Command and Data Handling Unit, a computer that "sends commands to Hubble's science instruments and formats science data for transmission to the ground," NASA said. The team "installed a soft capture mechanism, a device that will allow future vehicles to attach to the telescope," NASA said. And they installed "a combination of locks and latches that will allow for faster opening and closing of the telescope doors during the third spacewalk." "This is a huge accomplishment," Preston Burch, Hubble Space Telescope program manager, said during a briefing. "Our first EVA day in more than seven years." EVA is the acronym for "extravehicular activity," the phrase for spacewalking. It was the first of five spacewalks scheduled during the 11-day mission in which the crew will work in the shuttle's cargo bay to upgrade and repair Hubble. Astronauts Michael Good and Mike Massimino will perform the next spacewalk on Friday. They will be installing gyroscopes and batteries.  Learn more about the Hubble repairs » . The mission is one of the most ambitious space repair efforts ever attempted. Atlantis launched Monday afternoon for NASA's fifth and final repair visit to the telescope.  Watch Atlantis lift off on Hubble mission » . After a two-day chase, the shuttle captured the telescope Wednesday with its robotic arm some 350 miles above Earth and pulled it into Atlantis' cargo bay for service.  Watch Atlantis snag the Hubble » . It's been seven years since the last space shuttle crew worked on the telescope, which has been latched to a rotating, "lazy Susan"-type device for five days of repairs and remodeling. A camera mounted on the shuttle's robotic arm, 200 feet from the telescope, is taking pictures of it -- the first time the telescope has been seen since March 2002. An umbilical line was connected to provide electricity from Atlantis to the telescope, according to NASA. Mission commander Scott Altman also will position the shuttle to allow Hubble's solar arrays to gather energy from the sun and recharge the telescope's batteries. The timeline for the spacewalks is so tight, there's a chance the astronauts won't get everything done, especially if they hit any snags. And that's a real possibility because some of the repairs they are attempting have never been tried before. NASA canceled an Atlantis mission to extend Hubble's operational life in January 2004 because the trip was considered too risky in the wake of the 2003 space shuttle Columbia disaster, which killed seven astronauts. That accident was blamed on a hole punched in the front of the wing by debris during liftoff. But public pressure and steps taken to increase shuttle safety led the space agency to reconsider. Hubble's "greatest discoveries," NASA says, include determining the age of the universe -- 13.7 billion years, discovering that "virtually all major galaxies have black holes at their center," and "providing evidence that the speed at which the universe is expanding is accelerating -- caused by an unknown force that makes up for more than 75 percent of the universe." CNN's John Zarrella and Kim Segal contributed to this report .

# Atlantis astronauts complete first spacewalk of final Hubble mission

**SPACE CENTER, Houston (CNN)** — Two Atlantis astronauts completed the first spacewalk of NASA’s final Hubble Space Telescope servicing mission Thursday, overcoming a stubborn bolt to install a powerful new camera and replace a failed data-handling unit.

Veteran spacewalker John Grunsfeld and Andrew Feustel spent about seven hours and 20 minutes outside the shuttle during the first of five planned spacewalks on mission STS-125.

Their primary task was to remove Hubble’s Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and replace it with Wide Field Camera 3, an advanced instrument designed to observe the universe in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light.

The work briefly stalled when a bolt securing the old camera would not turn. After standard efforts failed, flight controllers authorized Grunsfeld to apply additional force. The bolt finally broke loose, allowing the astronauts to pull out the refrigerator-sized instrument and install its replacement.

The spacewalkers also replaced Hubble’s Science Instrument Command and Data Handling unit, the system that formats and routes scientific data from the telescope’s instruments. The original unit suffered an electrical failure in 2008, delaying the servicing mission while NASA prepared a replacement.

Atlantis launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on May 11, 2009, and captured Hubble with the shuttle’s robotic arm two days later. The first spacewalk took place May 14. Four more excursions were scheduled through May 18 to install the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph, repair the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph, replace gyroscopes and batteries, and add protective equipment.

The crew was expected to release Hubble on May 19 and return to Earth after completing the 13-day mission. Atlantis ultimately landed May 24 at Edwards Air Force Base in California after poor weather prevented a Florida landing.

The mission marked the fifth and final shuttle visit to Hubble. The telescope was launched aboard Discovery in April 1990, but astronauts later found that a flaw in its primary mirror blurred its images. A 1993 servicing crew installed corrective optics, transforming Hubble into one of NASA’s most productive scientific observatories.

STS-125 was initially canceled after the 2003 Columbia disaster because Hubble’s orbit did not allow the shuttle to reach the International Space Station in an emergency. NASA later reinstated the mission and placed Endeavour on standby for a possible rescue.

The seven-member Atlantis crew became the last people expected to visit Hubble. NASA said the upgrades and repairs were intended to extend the observatory’s scientific life for years, giving it greater observing power than at any previous point in its history.

# Atlantis Astronauts Complete First Spacewalk of High-Stakes Hubble Repair Mission

**May 14, 2009 — 6:30 p.m. EDT**

**HOUSTON** — Two spacewalking astronauts installed a powerful new camera and replaced a critical data-handling unit aboard the Hubble Space Telescope on Thursday, completing the first major phase of NASA’s most ambitious—and potentially dangerous—shuttle servicing mission.

John Grunsfeld and Andrew “Drew” Feustel worked outside the shuttle *Atlantis* for 7 hours and 20 minutes, beginning at 8:52 a.m. EDT and returning to the airlock at 4:12 p.m. Their principal achievement was the installation of Wide Field Camera 3, an advanced instrument designed to observe the universe in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light.

The astronauts also replaced Hubble’s Science Instrument Command and Data Handling unit, which directs commands to the telescope’s scientific instruments and formats their observations for transmission to Earth. The failure of the primary side of that unit in September 2008 forced NASA to delay the servicing flight and prepare a spare for launch.

Mission Control confirmed that the replacement electronics passed initial power checks. More extensive testing of the camera and data system will follow.

“Houston, WFC3 is installed,” Grunsfeld reported after the new camera was secured inside the telescope.

The work marked a strong start to five planned spacewalks intended to rebuild much of the 19-year-old observatory. If the mission succeeds, NASA expects Hubble to emerge with greater scientific capabilities than at any previous point in its history.

## A Stubborn Bolt Complicates Camera Replacement

The spacewalk was not without tense moments.

To make room for Wide Field Camera 3, Feustel had to remove Hubble’s Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, the refrigerator-sized instrument installed by astronauts during the first servicing mission in 1993. That camera produced many of Hubble’s best-known views, including the “Pillars of Creation” in the Eagle Nebula and a series of extremely deep surveys of distant galaxies.

A bolt securing the old camera initially resisted Feustel’s efforts. Engineers had imposed strict limits on the force astronauts could apply because a broken fastener or damaged mounting point could have jeopardized both removal and installation.

After consulting Mission Control and changing his technique, Feustel freed the bolt and carefully pulled the camera from its compartment. Mounted on the end of *Atlantis*’ robotic arm, he then guided the old instrument into a protective carrier in the shuttle’s payload bay.

Grunsfeld and Feustel removed Wide Field Camera 3 from its launch enclosure and slid it into the open instrument bay. The operation demanded careful alignment; Hubble’s instruments fit into narrow compartments and must connect precisely with electrical and data interfaces deep inside the telescope.

The new camera is expected to be far more sensitive than its predecessor, allowing astronomers to study some of the earliest galaxies, the birth and death of stars, the composition of planets and the behavior of dark matter and dark energy.

## Replacing Hubble’s Electronic “Nervous System”

The astronauts next turned to the replacement Science Instrument Command and Data Handling unit.

Hubble carries redundant electronics, but the September failure left the telescope operating on its backup side with no further reserve. NASA postponed the mission, originally scheduled for October 2008, so engineers could refurbish, test and prepare a replacement unit.

Installing it required the astronauts to disconnect and reconnect numerous electrical cables while wearing pressurized gloves. The work was especially important because a failure of the remaining operational system could have left Hubble unable to send most scientific data to Earth.

The successful initial activation removed one of the largest immediate threats to the observatory’s future.

## Why STS-125 Is So Ambitious

Designated STS-125, the mission is the fifth and final planned shuttle servicing visit to Hubble. NASA intends to accomplish in five spacewalks what would amount to a major overhaul of an observatory orbiting roughly 350 miles above Earth.

The crew plans to:

- Install Wide Field Camera 3 and the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph.
- Repair the Advanced Camera for Surveys and the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph.
- Replace Hubble’s aging gyroscopes and batteries.
- Install a new Fine Guidance Sensor.
- Replace degraded thermal insulation.
- Attach a docking mechanism that could allow a future robotic spacecraft to approach the telescope and eventually guide it to a controlled re-entry.

Some of the repairs are unprecedented. The Advanced Camera for Surveys and the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph were designed to be replaced as complete units, not opened and repaired by astronauts in orbit. Spacewalkers will have to remove covers and dozens of small fasteners while preventing screws or fragments from floating into the telescope.

NASA developed special tools, capture plates and work restraints for the task. The astronauts trained for years in large underwater mock-ups, but the actual repairs must be performed in bulky spacesuits, with limited visibility and little tolerance for error.

## No Safe Haven at the Space Station

The mission is also considered unusually risky because *Atlantis* cannot reach the International Space Station if it suffers serious damage.

Hubble and the station occupy orbits with sharply different inclinations to the equator. A shuttle at Hubble lacks enough fuel to change orbital planes and rendezvous with the station, eliminating the “safe haven” option available during station missions after the 2003 *Columbia* disaster.

NASA has therefore placed the shuttle *Endeavour* on standby at Kennedy Space Center. If inspections reveal damage that makes *Atlantis* unsafe for re-entry, *Endeavour* could launch on a rescue mission designated STS-400. The *Atlantis* astronauts would transfer between the two shuttles by spacewalk.

NASA is conducting detailed inspections of the shuttle’s heat shield using cameras and laser sensors. Hubble’s higher orbit also exposes *Atlantis* to a greater concentration of orbital debris than the station’s lower altitude.

The crew has limited supplies, making any rescue effort a race against time.

## A Scientific Observatory With Global Reach

Hubble was launched in April 1990 with a misshapen primary mirror that initially blurred its images. Astronauts corrected the flaw during the 1993 servicing mission, turning the telescope into one of the most productive scientific instruments ever built.

Above Earth’s atmosphere, Hubble can obtain unusually sharp images and observe wavelengths that are partly or completely blocked from ground-based telescopes. Its findings have helped astronomers refine the age and expansion rate of the universe, study the formation of galaxies, examine stellar nurseries and exploding stars, and gather evidence about the mysterious force known as dark energy.

The current overhaul is intended to extend Hubble’s life by at least several years and greatly expand its reach. Wide Field Camera 3 will provide broad imaging across an unusually wide range of wavelengths. The Cosmic Origins Spectrograph, scheduled for installation during a later spacewalk, will analyze faint ultraviolet light to reveal the chemical structure of matter between galaxies and trace how galaxies evolved.

Repairing the Advanced Camera for Surveys would restore one of Hubble’s most productive instruments. Reviving the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph would again allow astronomers to separate light into its component wavelengths, providing information about the motion, temperature and composition of distant objects.

The work is especially important because no direct replacement for Hubble is ready. NASA’s planned James Webb Space Telescope is intended primarily for infrared observations and will not duplicate all of Hubble’s ultraviolet and visible-light capabilities.

## Four Spacewalks Remain

Thursday’s success gives NASA an encouraging start, but much of the most delicate work remains.

Astronauts Michael Massimino and Michael Good are scheduled to conduct the second spacewalk, focusing on Hubble’s gyroscopes and batteries. Later excursions will include the installation of the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph and difficult internal repairs to the disabled imaging spectrograph and Advanced Camera for Surveys.

For Grunsfeld, an astronomer who has now visited Hubble three times, the mission carries particular significance. This is expected to be the last time astronauts touch the telescope.

After the first day’s work, Hubble remained firmly attached to *Atlantis*’ payload bay, its long solar arrays extending on either side as controllers prepared for the next stage of the orbital overhaul.

One successful spacewalk has given the telescope a new eye and a renewed electronic lifeline. Four more will determine whether Hubble can begin a final, more powerful chapter of discovery.

The mission’s five spacewalks were intended to extend Hubble’s useful life and greatly expand its scientific reach. In addition to the first day’s camera and computer replacements, later work was planned to install the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph, repair two instruments never designed for in-orbit servicing, replace gyroscopes and batteries, renew thermal protection and attach a mechanism for eventual robotic capture. Hubble had been launched in 1990, and STS-125 represented NASA’s last opportunity to overhaul it with shuttle astronauts.

# Atlantis leaves Hubble reborn after daring final servicing mission

**By Staff Science Correspondent**  
**EDWARDS AIR FORCE BASE, California — May 24, 2009**

Space Shuttle Atlantis returned to Earth on Sunday after capturing the Hubble Space Telescope and completing one of the most ambitious repair missions in the history of human spaceflight, giving the orbiting observatory new cameras, fresh batteries and what NASA hopes will be at least five more years of scientific life.

Atlantis touched down at Edwards Air Force Base in California at 8:39 a.m. Pacific time after bad weather prevented a landing at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The landing ended a 13-day mission in which seven astronauts rendezvoused with Hubble about 350 miles above Earth, seized it with the shuttle’s robotic arm and carried out five consecutive spacewalks.

“Hubble has been reborn,” mission specialist John Grunsfeld, an astronomer making his third trip to service the telescope, said after the astronauts completed their work.

The mission, designated STS-125, was the fifth and final shuttle visit to Hubble. It was also the first mission to the telescope since the 2003 loss of Columbia and its seven-member crew forced NASA to rethink how astronauts would inspect and protect a shuttle that could not reach the International Space Station.

Commander Scott Altman said the crew was leaving behind a telescope more capable than the one it had captured.

“It’s been an incredible voyage,” Altman told Mission Control shortly before Atlantis released Hubble. “The Hubble Space Telescope has been with us for nearly 20 years, and we’re giving it a new beginning.”

## A delicate capture in high orbit

Atlantis launched from Kennedy Space Center on May 11 and caught up with Hubble two days later. Unlike the International Space Station, Hubble has no docking port for a shuttle. Astronaut Megan McArthur therefore used Atlantis’s 50-foot robotic arm to grapple a fixture on the telescope as the two spacecraft flew around Earth at roughly 17,500 mph.

“Houston, Atlantis, Hubble has arrived on board Atlantis,” Altman reported after the capture.

The telescope was then lowered onto a rotating work platform in Atlantis’s payload bay. The platform held Hubble steady and supplied electrical power while the astronauts opened equipment bays and removed instruments that had not been designed for easy repair in orbit.

Hubble is approximately 43 feet long, 14 feet wide and weighs about 24,500 pounds. Launched by Space Shuttle Discovery in April 1990, it circles above most of Earth’s atmosphere, allowing its 7.9-foot primary mirror to observe the universe without the blurring and absorption that affect ground-based telescopes.

The observatory’s high orbit made the servicing mission particularly challenging. Hubble flies well above the space station, in a region where Atlantis faced increased exposure to small pieces of orbital debris. The telescope’s orbital inclination also meant the shuttle could not divert to the station if its heat shield suffered serious damage.

## Five spacewalks, two new instruments

Working in pairs, astronauts Grunsfeld, Andrew Feustel, Michael Good and Michael Massimino spent a combined 36 hours and 56 minutes outside Atlantis during five spacewalks.

Their principal task was to install two new scientific instruments.

The **Wide Field Camera 3**, or WFC3, replaced Hubble’s Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, which had been in orbit since 1993. The new camera can observe ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light, giving astronomers a broader view of everything from nearby planets to some of the earliest galaxies.

The astronauts also installed the **Cosmic Origins Spectrograph**, designed to separate ultraviolet light into its component wavelengths. Scientists expect it to study the large-scale web of gas between galaxies, the chemical evolution of the universe and the material surrounding distant quasars.

The mission also attempted something never envisioned when Hubble was built: repairing complex science instruments in space at the circuit-board level.

Astronauts restored the **Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph**, which had stopped operating in 2004, by removing dozens of tiny fasteners and replacing a failed electronics board. They also repaired one of the main channels of the **Advanced Camera for Surveys**, disabled by an electrical failure in 2007.

The work required specially developed tools, fastener-capture plates and careful procedures to prevent screws or sharp fragments from floating into the payload bay.

Massimino’s repair of the imaging spectrograph provided the mission’s most dramatic mechanical setback. A screw holding a handrail refused to turn, blocking access to an electronics panel. After engineers on the ground determined that greater force would not endanger the telescope, Massimino pulled the handrail free by hand.

“There was no other option,” Massimino later recalled. “We had to get that handrail off to get to the instrument.”

The astronauts covered the area to contain possible debris and continued the repair. Tests later showed that the spectrograph had returned to operation.

## New gyroscopes, batteries and insulation

Beyond the science instruments, the crew replaced all six of Hubble’s gyroscopes, which measure the telescope’s motion and help it point with extraordinary precision. Hubble normally uses three gyroscopes during scientific observations, although engineers have developed operating modes that require only one or two.

The astronauts also installed six new nickel-hydrogen batteries. Hubble relies on batteries while passing through Earth’s shadow, recharging them with its solar arrays during daylight portions of each 96-minute orbit.

Other work included replacing a Fine Guidance Sensor, fitting new thermal-insulation panels and installing a device known as the **Soft Capture Mechanism**. The mechanism is intended to make it easier for a future robotic spacecraft to attach to Hubble and guide it safely out of orbit when the telescope can no longer operate.

Hubble has no propulsion system capable of conducting a controlled re-entry on its own. Without intervention, atmospheric drag will eventually lower its orbit, although the timing depends heavily on solar activity and the resulting expansion of Earth’s upper atmosphere.

NASA officials said preliminary checks indicated that the repaired telescope was healthy. Full calibration of the new and restored instruments was expected to take several months.

## Columbia shaped every decision

The shadow of the Columbia disaster hung over the mission from its earliest planning stages.

Columbia broke apart during re-entry on Feb. 1, 2003, killing commander Rick Husband, pilot William McCool, payload commander Michael Anderson, mission specialists Kalpana Chawla, David Brown and Laurel Clark, and Israeli payload specialist Ilan Ramon.

Investigators found that a piece of insulating foam had broken away from Columbia’s external fuel tank during launch and struck the leading edge of the shuttle’s left wing. The impact opened a breach that allowed superheated gas to enter the wing during re-entry.

After the accident, NASA developed extensive in-orbit inspection and repair procedures. Shuttle crews began using cameras and laser sensors mounted on a long boom to examine the nose cap and the reinforced carbon-carbon panels along the wing edges.

Atlantis’s crew carried out those inspections after launch and again before landing. Engineers studied several areas where launch debris had damaged heat-shield tiles but concluded that none posed a threat.

The inability to seek refuge aboard the space station created another complication. NASA placed Space Shuttle Endeavour on a second launch pad with a four-astronaut rescue crew prepared for a mission known as STS-400. If Atlantis had been judged unable to return safely, Endeavour would have rendezvoused with it and transferred the stranded astronauts by spacewalk.

No such rescue was required, and Endeavour was released from standby after Atlantis’s heat shield passed its final inspections.

The rescue preparations, repeated inspections and changes to the external tank were direct consequences of Columbia. They also reflected the debate over whether a Hubble mission was worth placing another shuttle crew beyond the reach of the space station.

NASA initially canceled the servicing flight in 2004, saying it could not meet post-Columbia safety requirements. The agency later restored the mission after engineers developed new inspection techniques, repair options and the standby-rescue plan.

## A telescope that changed astronomy

The determination to save Hubble reflected its scientific record as much as its symbolic importance.

Hubble’s first images in 1990 were blurred by a manufacturing error in its primary mirror. The defect was only about one-fiftieth the thickness of a human hair, but it prevented the telescope from focusing light as designed. Astronauts corrected the problem during the first servicing mission in 1993 by installing corrective optics and a new camera.

Since then, Hubble has helped transform astronomers’ understanding of the universe.

Among its most influential achievements:

- **Measuring the expansion rate of the universe:** Observations of Cepheid variable stars helped the Hubble Key Project refine the Hubble constant, narrowing estimates of the universe’s age and expansion rate.

- **Evidence for an accelerating universe:** Hubble observations of distant supernovae helped strengthen the conclusion that cosmic expansion is speeding up, a finding attributed to the still-mysterious phenomenon called dark energy.

- **The Hubble Deep Fields:** By staring at apparently empty patches of sky for days, Hubble revealed thousands of galaxies, some seen as they existed when the universe was only a small fraction of its present age.

- **Supermassive black holes:** Measurements of stars and gas in galactic centers showed that enormous black holes are common and that their masses are linked to properties of their host galaxies.

- **Exoplanet atmospheres:** Hubble detected elements and molecules in the atmospheres of planets orbiting other stars, helping to establish the study of exoplanet weather and chemistry.

- **Star birth and death:** Images such as the “Pillars of Creation” in the Eagle Nebula documented towering clouds of gas and dust where stars are forming. Other observations captured planetary nebulae, supernova remnants and the violent final stages of stellar evolution.

- **A changing solar system:** Hubble watched the fragments of Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 crash into Jupiter in 1994 and has repeatedly monitored weather, auroras and atmospheric changes on the outer planets.

Because light takes time to travel, Hubble’s most distant observations also function as views into the past. The new instruments installed by Atlantis were designed in part to push that record farther back, toward the period when the first galaxies formed.

## The last human visit

Atlantis released Hubble on May 19. McArthur lifted the telescope out of the payload bay with the robotic arm and let it go as the shuttle and observatory passed over the Atlantic Ocean.

Grunsfeld, who had spent years working on Hubble both as an astronaut and astronomer, offered a final salute.

“Hubble is not just a satellite,” he said. “It’s about humanity’s quest for knowledge.”

After the release, Atlantis fired its maneuvering engines and moved away, leaving Hubble to resume its solitary orbit. The telescope’s solar arrays turned toward the Sun as controllers at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore began checking its systems.

NASA expects to retire the shuttle fleet after completing assembly of the International Space Station. As a result, no further astronaut servicing mission to Hubble is planned.

The telescope’s eventual lifetime will depend on the health of its new components and the gradual decay of its orbit. But with fresh batteries, six new gyroscopes, two advanced instruments and two repaired instruments, engineers believe Hubble could remain scientifically productive well into the next decade.

For the Atlantis crew, the mission combined precision engineering with the knowledge that no astronauts are likely to touch Hubble again.

Standing on the runway after landing, Altman praised both his crew and the teams that had spent years preparing the repairs.

“Hubble’s going to continue to rewrite the textbooks,” he said. “We’re just happy we could give it the chance.”
